newsitem.title: USA: NYS' Silver declines to tip his hand on LIPA pact.
newsitem.headline: NYS' Silver declines to tip his hand on LIPA pact.

text.p: The New York State Assembly Speaker on Wednesday declined to disclose whether he would veto one of Gov George Pataki's most ambitious plans, a $7.3 billion proposal to cut Long Island's electricity rates.

Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, told reporters in Albany the plan must be judged on its merits, again noting that the Assembly, which has held a series of public hearings, has questions about whether the transaction would capture all the savings that have been estimated.

Asked if he would ask the Republican governor to modify his proposal, which calls for a partial state takeover of the Long Island Lighting Co, Silver replied "I have to make a determination whether changing the deal would make it more attractive or not."

Silver, along with Pataki and the Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, hold the three seats on the state board that must approve all agency debt sales. The Public Authorities Control Board next meets July 16, and while Pataki's plan is on the schedule, it still could be pulled.
The deal would be paid for with the nation's biggest-ever municipal bond sale, giving the Long Island Power Authority the money to buy assets from LILCO and Brooklyn Union Gas, which plan to merge.

Long Island residents now pay some of the highest electricity prices in the nation, and Pataki says the deal would cut their rates by 17 percent. He dismissed his Democrat opponent's views, saying that if the plan were judged on the merits, the Democrat-led Assembly would approve it. "We've answered all their questions; now's the time for them to vote."
Opponents of the governor's plan have speculated that the LIPA deal might get caught up in the state's budget talks, which hit their 100th day without achieving a pact.

The Senate Majority Leader, asked if Silver had sought to include the LIPA transaction in the budget, denied he had done so. "No. Nobody is saying that anything that's outside the budget has to be linked." In previous budget negotiations, lawmakers, including Pataki, have held up the budget in an effort to wring concesssions out of their opponents on other policies.
